name: World Humanoid Robot Games
ability_definition: The ability to use short bursts of muscle force to propel oneself (as in jumping or sprinting), or to throw an object.

task_realism.reasoning: The standing high jump, standing long jump, 100 m sprint and obstacle race are the same short-burst tasks the ability definition names. Physical robots must generate the force themselves. Workplace explosive-strength demands differ somewhat: sprinting to respond, jumping onto or over obstacles, heaving or tossing objects. Those usually come with loads, uneven terrain and task goals that stylized track-and-field events lack.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Measurement is standardized and physical, on real hardware under fixed rules. However, autonomous and teleoperated robots were mixed, and a 0.8 time coefficient made sprint times ambiguous. It is also unconfirmed whether the reported jump was autonomous. There has been only one edition, with no official consolidated leaderboard. The controlled arena, flat surfaces and lack of repeated efforts, fatigue or real stakes diverge from workplace conditions.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers two of the three components in the definition: jumping, both vertical and horizontal, and sprinting and acceleration. It entirely omits throwing an object. It also does not assess explosive effort while carrying loads or in varied directions. The reported result is a single event, not a composite.

format_match.reasoning: Outputs are real physical performances measured in physical units: centimeters jumped and seconds sprinted. This is the natural way explosive strength is assessed in humans. There are no proxy formats or simulated rewards. The only deduction is for the sprint-time adjustment ambiguity, which reduces interpretability of some results.

transferability_reasoning: The World Humanoid Robot Games directly measures jumping and sprinting on physical humanoids in physical units, so its task realism and format match to the explosive-strength ability are strong. Transfer is limited by the absence of throwing, the narrow track-and-field framing, and messy evaluation conditions: mixed teleoperation, time coefficients, a single edition and no official leaderboard. Together these weaken how well results reflect real autonomous workplace capability.

2025.model_or_system: Robotera (Xingdong Era) Xingdong L7 humanoid robot
2025.human_reference: General adult workforce (physically active workers for whom explosive strength matters, e.g., laborers, first responders, warehouse staff), not trained jumpers

2026.model_or_system: Tiangong Ultra (Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center)
2026.metric: seconds (100 m sprint time, large-size robot final; lower is better)
2026.human_reference: Working adults whose jobs call for short bursts of maximal force, such as laborers, firefighters, law enforcement, military and athletes. The median member is an untrained or moderately fit adult who runs 100 m in roughly 14-17 s.
